messages.content: One area I'd like to fill in: beyond the dual IATF/ISO certifications and the cleanroom, what would you say is the single biggest reason customers choose Great Lakes over other injection molders?

The tool room.

We've had our own tool room since 1994 — nine guys now, led by Greg Tomczak, who's been here 24 years. Most molders outsource all their mold maintenance or they've got maybe two toolmakers who can swap a slide or change a gate. We can build inserts, modify cavities, run mold-flow on a repair, cut EDM work in-house, and turn around a breakdown in hours instead of days.

Maumee Valley told us flat-out in 2017 that's why they consolidated three programs with us — their previous molder shipped molds to a third party in Michigan every time something broke, and it killed their launch schedule. Our tool room keeps the presses running, and when a customer needs a dimension tweaked or a gate relocated after first article, we do it here without the three-week turnaround.

That and the fact that my father taught every one of our people that the customer's production schedule is sacred.
How much of your current tooling do you own outright versus customer-owned molds that you store and maintain?

We own maybe 15–18 molds outright — mostly older low-runner parts where the customer went away or we bought the tool out at end-of-life. Everything else is customer-owned; we store it, maintain it, and run it under the supply agreements.

The customer-owned molds probably number around 240–250 active tools, though Rob keeps the exact list. Some are single-cavity prototype molds, some are 16-cavity production families. We've got racking for about 300 molds in the tool room and overflow in the back warehouse.

We charge the customer for major repairs — anything over routine PM — and that's in the supply agreements. Routine maintenance like cleaning, minor gate work, ejector pins, that's on us and it's baked into the piece price.
How concentrated is the customer-owned tooling — do any of the top five customers own 40% or more of those 240–250 molds?

Let me take those mold numbers back — I was guessing, and I don't want a guess ending up in the book. Rob keeps the tooling list with owner and customer for every mold; he can send it over. What I do know is nearly all of it is customer-owned, which is normal for us.

On a related note: when a customer's program ends or they decide to move production, do the supply agreements require you to return the mold within a set timeframe, or do you have any leverage to hold it until outstanding invoices are settled?

The supply agreements say we return the mold "within a reasonable time" after the customer requests it — usually 30 days. We've got a lien right under Ohio law for unpaid invoices or tooling work, so we can hold a mold if there's an outstanding balance, but we've only done that twice in 30 years and one of them turned into the lawsuit we settled last June.

Most of the time when a program ends the customer either asks us to scrap the mold or they leave it here on the rack indefinitely because moving it and re-validating somewhere else costs more than the program's worth. We've got probably 40 or 50 inactive molds sitting in the back that nobody's touched in five years.
Switching to your press fleet — your asset list shows 38 presses ranging from 55 to 720 tons. What's your current overall utilization rate across the fleet?

About 72% in 2024. The cleanroom presses run closer to 85–90% because those medical programs are sticky and validated. The main floor has more variability — automotive schedules, model changeovers, that July shutdown.

We've got capacity to add maybe $10 million in revenue without buying another press, which is one reason a buyer should like this business.
What's the age breakdown on the 38 presses — roughly how many are under 10 years old, 10–20 years, and over 20?

Rob's got the exact list with serial numbers and install dates, but roughly: the 14 all-electrics are all newer — the oldest is maybe 2015, most are 2019 or later. The 8 hybrids are mid-range, call it 10–15 years. The hydraulics are the mix — maybe half are under 15 years, but we've got about 10 hydraulics that are over 20 years old and those are the ones we're replacing two or three at a time as budget allows.

The old hydraulics still run fine for non-critical parts, but they're maintenance hogs and the power consumption is terrible compared to the electrics.

On resin — you mentioned two main distributors plus a direct medical-grade supplier. How do your pricing arrangements work: are you on fixed annual contracts, index-based pricing that passes resin volatility to customers, or somewhere in between?

Automotive is mostly pass-through but it lags about a quarter, which can hurt us when resin spikes fast. The Tier-1 supply agreements have a resin-adjustment clause — we submit invoices showing the resin cost change and they true it up on the next quarter's PO, but there's always that 60–90 day gap where we're eating the difference.

Medical is cleaner: resin-index pricing tied to a published benchmark, adjusted quarterly. If the index goes up 8%, the piece price goes up 8% on the resin portion. Veridian, Clearwater, Halvorsen — they all have that in the supply agreements.

Tom can walk you through the exact mechanics of the index formula; I just know it works and we don't get squeezed the way we do on automotive.
When resin spiked in 2021–22, how much margin compression did you see on the automotive side during those lag periods — rough percentage points or dollar impact?

That's a Tom question — I don't remember the exact margin hit by quarter. What I do remember is we had to draw on the revolver for the first time in years just to cover working capital because we were buying resin at spot prices that were 30–40% higher than what we were billing the customers for three months prior.

It smoothed out by mid-2022 once prices stabilized, but it was tight for about nine months.

I'll flag that as something Tom can quantify for the financial package.

Shifting to your workforce: with the 30% annual turnover on operators, what's your current approach to recruiting and training — are you relying on temp agencies, direct hiring, in-house training programs, or a mix?

It's 29%, and yeah, it's all of the above. We run about 15 temps through Quillon Staffing at any given time — they're a screen, and if somebody shows up on time for 90 days and can follow a setup sheet we offer them direct. Maybe one in three converts.

Direct hires come from Indeed, referral bonuses ($500 if your buddy stays six months), and we've got a partnership with the Penta Career Center where their plastics students do a co-op here senior year. Luis runs a two-week in-house training program — safety, quality, how to read a work order, basic troubleshooting — and then they shadow a lead operator for another two weeks before they're on their own.

The turnover's mostly in the first six months; once they make it past a year they tend to stay.
What about your skilled trades — setup technicians and toolmakers? What does turnover look like there, and how deep is your bench if Greg decides to retire?

Setup techs and toolmakers almost never leave — maybe one every two or three years. Greg's the issue: he's 61, wants to retire in 2027, and we don't have a ready replacement yet.

The leading candidate is Nate Szymanski, 34, been a toolmaker here for eight years, but he's not at Greg's level — Greg can diagnose a mold problem by listening to the press cycle, and he's the one who trains everybody. We've talked about bringing in a senior toolmaker from outside before Greg leaves, but we haven't pulled the trigger yet, and honestly that's something a buyer with a bigger tool-room network could solve faster than we can.

That's a candid assessment — and buyers will want to understand the succession plan for the tool room, so flagging it proactively is the right move.

Stepping back to quality: your 18 PPM and Gold supplier status with Maumee Valley are strong, but IATF 16949 recertification is coming up fall 2026. Have you started the pre-audit prep, and are there any findings from the last surveillance audit that you're still working through?

The October 2024 surveillance had zero majors and three minors — two were documentation gaps in APQP on a new program, one was a calibration record that wasn't signed off on time. All three closed by December.

Sandra's already building the timeline for the October 2026 recertification audit — we'll do an internal audit in May or June 2026 and a pre-assessment with Northstar probably in August. We've never failed an IATF audit and we're not going to start now, but yeah, a buyer needs to know that recert is sitting right there six months after closing if we close in Q1 2026.

That's one reason I want to close before summer — I don't want a new owner walking into a recertification audit three months after they take the keys.
On the ISO 13485 side for medical: when was your last surveillance audit, and are there any open CAPAs or observations from that one?

February 2025 — about three months ago. Zero majors, two minors: one was a training record for a new cleanroom operator that wasn't complete before she started running production (we caught it in our internal audit first), and the other was a customer complaint log where we didn't document the root cause analysis within the timeframe in our own procedure.

Both closed in March. No open CAPAs from the registrar; we've got maybe a dozen internal CAPAs in the system at any given time but that's normal — most are from our own internal audits or process improvements, not customer complaints.

On your medical device business specifically: beyond Veridian, Clearwater, and Halvorsen, are there any new programs currently in the quoting stage or early NPI that could add meaningful revenue in the next 12–18 months?

The Veridian catheter hub is the big one — nominated in February, tooling PO just came in, start of production Q1 2026, about $1.8 million a year at full rate.

Beyond that we've got three or four other medical RFQs out — an IVD cartridge housing, a respiratory nebulizer component, something for a dental device company — but nothing awarded yet. Medical sales cycles are long; you quote, they validate your process, they audit you, then maybe 18 months later you get a PO.

The medical pipeline is healthy but it's not like automotive where you can win a program and be in production in six months.

That $1.8 million Veridian catheter hub program is meaningful — close to 3% of current revenue once it's at full rate.

On the automotive side, what does your current platform exposure look like? Specifically, how much of your automotive revenue is tied to EV programs versus traditional ICE vehicles?

EV is still small for us — maybe 10–12% of automotive revenue, mostly the high-voltage connector housings we do for Northgate. That piece grew about 10% in 2024 but it's off a small base.

The rest is a mix: about 40% of the Lakeshore volume is ICE under-hood parts like fluid connectors and clips, but the other 60% is powertrain-agnostic — brake reservoir caps, coolant fittings, that kind of thing. Maumee Valley is all interior trim, so that's platform-agnostic. Kestrel is lighting brackets, Arbor is seating — none of that cares whether it's gas or electric.

We're not heavily exposed to ICE drivetrains, but we're also not riding the EV wave the way some molders are.

That powertrain-agnostic mix is actually a strength — reduces the risk of a rapid ICE decline hitting you hard.

One more on the automotive contracts: when a program ends — say a model changeover or a Tier-1 consolidates suppliers — what does the exit look like? Do your supply agreements have termination-for-convenience clauses with a notice period, or are you generally protected through the model year?

Most of the long-term supply agreements have termination-for-convenience with 90 to 180 days' notice, but in practice the Tier-1s give us a rolling 12-month forecast and we know when a platform is sunsetting.

When a program ends it's usually end-of-production for that vehicle model — the customer doesn't yank it mid-cycle unless we screw up quality, which we don't. They'll give us six months' notice, we run out the service parts for another year or two at lower volumes, and then it's done.

The risk is always that they don't award us the replacement program on the next platform, and that's where the 1.5% annual price-downs hurt — if we've been grinding margin for five years and then they re-source it to someone cheaper, we just lost the revenue with nothing behind it.
Has that happened recently — a program where you weren't awarded the replacement after the model sunsetted?

Yeah. Maumee Valley program MV-417, a door-trim bezel — it ends production in December 2026, about $2.1 million a year. We quoted two replacement programs for the next platform and we're still waiting to hear, probably this summer.

It's not that we lost the customer — Maumee Valley's still our biggest account and the relationship's fine — it's just how the automotive cycle works. Programs end, you quote the new ones, sometimes you win, sometimes you don't.

That's a helpful reality check on automotive program lifecycle — and the fact that you're still in the running for replacement programs shows the relationship is intact.

On your medical contracts: what are the typical terms and minimum volume commitments? Do they look more like the automotive supply agreements with termination-for-convenience, or are they structured differently given the validation requirements?

Medical contracts are stickier because of the validation — if Veridian wants to move that catheter hub to another molder, they have to revalidate the whole process at the new supplier, which can take six months and cost them a couple hundred thousand dollars. So the supply agreements are usually three years with auto-renewal, and there's no termination-for-convenience without cause.

The flip side is there's no minimum volume commitment either — it's a supply agreement, not a take-or-pay contract. If their product sales tank, our volumes drop, but as long as they're selling the device they're buying from us.

We've never had a medical customer pull a program for price or quality; the only time we've lost medical revenue is when a customer's product failed in the market or they got acquired and the new parent moved everything in-house.

One thing I want to make sure we capture: if you were to sell via a stock deal versus an asset deal, do any of your key customer agreements require formal consent for assignment, or just notice of a change in control?

Tom and our attorney went through this when we engaged Morgan. Most of the automotive supply agreements have a change-of-control clause that requires notice but not consent — we tell them we were acquired, introduce the new owner, keep running.

A couple of the medical contracts — Veridian and I think Clearwater — have a consent-to-assign clause, but the attorney said that's usually a formality as long as the buyer is qualified (same certifications, same facility, same key people for a transition period). We've never tested it because we've never sold before, but the expectation is they're not going to say no if the buyer's a credible medical molder.

The one we'd have to watch is if a buyer wanted to move the medical work offshore or shut down the cleanroom — that would probably trigger a fight.

On that Veridian consent requirement specifically — if this were structured as a stock sale or an F-reorganization rather than an asset sale, would the consent-to-assign clause still trigger, or does it only apply to asset deals?

I'd have to ask the attorney — I don't know the legal difference there. My understanding is a stock sale means the same corporation owns the contracts so maybe it doesn't trigger, but I'm not sure.

Tom or Morgan would know.

That's the kind of detail the attorney can confirm — in most cases stock deals avoid triggering assignment clauses, but it depends on the exact contract language. I'll note it for the broker to verify.

Shifting to FDA requirements: is Great Lakes registered as a medical device establishment with the FDA, and are any of the parts you mold listed under your customers' 510(k) filings, or do you operate purely as a contract manufacturer under their registrations?

We're not registered with the FDA — we're a component supplier, not a device manufacturer. The customers hold the 510(k)s and the registrations; we're listed as a contract manufacturer in their design history files and their supplier audits, but the regulatory burden is on them.

Veridian, Clearwater, Halvorsen — they all audit us annually under their quality agreements, and we have to notify them if we change a process or move a mold to a different press, but we're not the manufacturer of record.

That's pretty standard for injection molders in the medical space unless you're making the finished device and putting it in a box with your name on it.

That clarifies the regulatory picture — component suppliers typically stay off FDA's direct radar while still meeting the quality system requirements through customer audits.

One last area I want to touch: are there any environmental permits for the facility — air quality, wastewater discharge, or hazardous waste handling — that a buyer would need to transfer or reapply for?

We've got an air registration with the Toledo Division of Environmental Services for the resin dryers and the regrind system — it's a minor source permit, not a Title V. No wastewater discharge permit because we're on city sewer and we don't do any washing or plating. Hazardous waste is just used oil and empty resin containers, and we've got a small-quantity generator EPA ID number — our waste hauler picks up quarterly.

The Phase I environmental site assessment from 2019 came back clean. We've never done painting, plating, or anything that would leave contamination, and the site was vacant land before we built in 1994.

Jamal Whitfield, our maintenance supervisor, handles all the permit renewals and the waste manifests — it's pretty straightforward.

We've covered a lot of ground today. Before we wrap, is there anything about the business — a strength, a risk, a nuance in how things work — that you think a buyer needs to understand that we haven't touched on?

The people. My father started this company with four beat-up presses and a handshake, and the reason we're still here 38 years later is that our people show up every day and give a damn about the customer's parts. Luis has been here 16 years, Greg 24, Sandra 7 — we've got shift leads who've been running the same presses for a decade.

A buyer who comes in here and treats this like a balance sheet is going to lose that, and once you lose it in manufacturing you don't get it back. The buyer who understands that this is a people business with machines, not the other way around — that's the buyer who's going to make this work and grow it.

And yeah, we need capital for the second cleanroom and automation, but we also need an owner who's going to be here, not run it from a spreadsheet in New York.

I'll make sure that comes through.

We've covered a lot of ground: the tool room as a competitive moat, press fleet and utilization, resin pass-through mechanics, workforce structure and the Greg succession question, quality certifications and the 2026 recert timeline, automotive versus medical contract dynamics, the Veridian consent question, FDA positioning, and environmental permits.

A few items I'll flag for follow-up: Tom can quantify the 2021–22 resin margin compression, Rob has the exact tooling list, and your attorney can confirm the stock-versus-asset consent trigger on Veridian and Clearwater. Otherwise, I think we're in good shape.

Anything else you want to add, or are we good to close out for today?

We're good. Thanks for taking the time to understand the business — most people just want the financials and the customer list. I appreciate that you dug into the tool room and the people side.

Let me know if Morgan needs anything else from me or if Tom needs to pull together more numbers. I want this done right.

Thank you, Diane. This conversation gave me a much clearer picture of what makes Great Lakes tick — the tool room capability, the culture your father built, and the operational discipline that shows up in your quality numbers and customer retention. That's the story buyers need to hear alongside the financials.

I'll get this to Morgan with the follow-up items flagged: Tom on the resin margin data, Rob on the tooling list, and your attorney on the Veridian/Clearwater consent language. If anything else comes up, we know where to find you.

Good luck with the process — and I hope you find that buyer who understands it's a people business.
Welcome back, Diane. On the employee side, how is your quality department structured — how many people report to Sandra Okafor, and do any of them hold specific certifications like CQE or CQA?

Sandra has 16 people total: probably 10 or 11 inspectors on the floor across the three shifts doing first-piece, in-process and final inspection, then 3 quality engineers who handle CAPAs and customer audits and process validation, and a couple lab techs who run the CMMs and do dimensional reports.

As far as certifications, Sandra's got her ASQ CQA — Certified Quality Auditor — and I think one of the engineers has a CQE but I'm not positive. The inspectors don't need formal certs; we train them in-house on GD&T, how to read a print, how to use calipers and micrometers, and then they get qualified on each part family.

Sandra's the ISO 13485 management rep, so she owns the whole quality system and she reports directly to me.
What's Sandra's tenure with the company, and has she indicated any plans to stay or leave after a sale?

Seven years — she came from a Tier-1 supplier in 2018. I haven't told her about the sale yet; only Tom, Rob, Karen and Morgan know.

My plan is to tell Sandra and Luis and Megan once we have an LOI, maybe a month before we announce it to the whole company. Sandra's solid and I think she'll stay if the buyer treats her right and keeps investing in quality, but I can't promise that until I know who the buyer is.
Who is Megan, and what's her role?

Megan Pryor — Director of Sales and Program Management. She's been here five years, came from a big Tier-1. She owns quoting, customer program launches, and the customer-facing side of new business.

She works with the engineers to cost out RFQs, negotiates piece prices with the customers, and then hands off to the program managers once we win. She's also the one who rebuilt our quoting process in 2021 so we're not leaving margin on the table the way we used to.

I haven't told her about the sale either, but she'll need to know before closing because she's the face of the company to a lot of these customers.
How many program managers report to Megan, and is she involved in the day-to-day customer relationships or primarily on the front-end quoting and launch side?

Two program managers report to her — one handles automotive accounts, the other handles medical and industrial. They own the ongoing customer relationship, the forecasts, schedule changes, that stuff. Megan's mostly front-end: quoting, contract negotiation, PPAP launches, and she steps in if there's an escalation or a big customer audit.

She also still carries a couple of the smaller accounts herself where we don't have enough volume to justify a dedicated program manager.

Shifting to the operations side — your documents show about $2.9 million in capital expenditure last year. What would you estimate as the normalized annual maintenance capex to keep the presses and facility in good shape, separate from growth investments like the cleanroom expansion?

About $1.6 million a year just to keep the lights on — replace a couple of old hydraulics, rebuild a screw and barrel here and there, upgrade a chiller or a dryer, fix the roof when it leaks. That's maintenance capex.

The $2.9 million in 2024 included two new all-electric cleanroom presses, which were growth, not maintenance. Same thing in 2023 — the cleanroom expansion and the four electrics pushed that year up to $3.4 million, but the baseline is closer to $1.6 million if you're not adding capacity.

On the real estate side — your financials show the building appraised at $8.6 million in 2023, and I've seen the leaseback option sketched at around $6.50 per square foot. What's the age and condition of the roof, and has there been any significant deferred maintenance on the building itself?

The west roof section is original to 1994 — it's a 30-year roof and it's at the end of its life. We've got a quote for about $380,000 to replace it; we were planning to do it in 2025 or '26.

The east roof got repaired in 2023 after a hailstorm — that's the $96,800 add-back in the 2023 financials, net of insurance. The chillers were replaced in 2021, the cleanroom HVAC in 2023. Otherwise the building's in good shape — it's a steel frame with block walls, nothing fancy, but it's solid.

If a buyer takes the building they need to budget for that west roof pretty soon.
What's the electrical capacity at the facility — are you close to maxed out, or is there headroom for additional presses or a second cleanroom without a major utility upgrade?

We've got a 2,000-amp service and we're using maybe 70–75% of it. Jamal says we've got room for another 8 to 10 presses before we'd need to upgrade the service, and the second cleanroom wouldn't push us over — the HVAC for a cleanroom pulls a lot but it's not like adding a 500-ton press.

The bigger constraint for a second cleanroom is the chilled water capacity — we'd probably need to add another chiller or upsize the cooling tower, but that's a $200–250,000 problem, not a million-dollar utility upgrade.
Who supplies your resin, and do you have any concentration risk there — is it one distributor, or are you spread across multiple sources?

I already answered that — Midwest Polymer is about 38%, Keystone about 27%, Aurelian direct for the medical-grade resins maybe 15%, and the rest is smaller suppliers and colorant. No single supplier over 40%.

We've got good relationships with all three and we play them off each other a little bit on price, but resin's a commodity so there's only so much leverage.

You're right — I had that from earlier. On the automotive side, a couple of your programs run ICE-specific components and some are EV. Roughly what percentage of your automotive revenue is tied to EV platforms versus traditional ICE drivetrains versus parts that are platform-agnostic?
I think that covers it — let's wrap up here. Tom can send anything else you need.

Understood — we've covered a lot of ground today. You've given me a clear picture of the quality organization, the sales and program management structure, maintenance capex versus growth investments, the facility condition and utility headroom, and the key people who'll need to be part of the transition.

I'll follow up with Tom on the 2021–22 resin margin data and with Rob on the complete tooling list. Everything else is saved, and you can pick this up anytime if there's more to add. Thank you, Diane.

ZOOM MEETING TRANSCRIPT (auto-generated, lightly cleaned)
Meeting: Clearwater Physiotherapy - working session (Brassline Advisory Partners)
Date: Tuesday, February 10, 2026, 10:00 AM MST / 12:00 PM EST
Duration: 40:12
Platform: Zoom
Participants:
  Morgan Ellis - Senior Advisor, Brassline Advisory Partners (Toronto)
  Dr. Amrit Sandhu - Owner & Clinical Director, Clearwater Physiotherapy & Wellness Inc. (Calgary, Hillhurst clinic back office)

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

[00:00:04] Morgan Ellis: Morning, Amrit. Can you hear me okay?

[00:00:07] Amrit Sandhu: I can. Give me a second, the camera's pointing at the ceiling. There we go. Sorry, I'm in the back office at Hillhurst. It's the only room without a plinth in it.

[00:00:15] Morgan Ellis: That works. How's the weather out there?

[00:00:18] Amrit Sandhu: We've got a chinook, so it's plus nine today and it'll be minus twenty on Thursday. Good for business, honestly. Everybody slips on the ice once the melt freezes again. That's a bit dark, but it's true. January and February are always busy for us.

[00:00:31] Morgan Ellis: (laughs) We'll put it in the seasonality section more politely. So the plan today: I've got your statements, the T2s, the leases and Dana's two spreadsheets. They're clean and they tie together, which is rare. Today I want the story, the things that aren't on paper. Then we'll get you into the Cimple interview, and that'll capture the rest in more detail. Sound okay?

[00:00:52] Amrit Sandhu: Sounds good. Dana will be thrilled you said her spreadsheets are clean.

[00:00:56] Morgan Ellis: Let's start at the beginning. How did Clearwater start?

[00:01:02] Amrit Sandhu: Okay. I qualified as a physio in 1999, so that's, wow, twenty-six years ago. I did hospital outpatient work for years and then worked at a couple of private clinics. I did my PhD part-time, in rehab science, and finished in 2008. By then I'd worked for other people long enough to have strong opinions about how a clinic should run. So in March 2009 my wife Harjit and I incorporated. We opened in a little 1,900-square-foot space in Hillhurst, a few blocks from where we are now. It was me, two other physios and one massage therapist, Aimee, who is still with us. She's been here since 2011, actually. I'm getting the order mixed up.

[00:01:48] Morgan Ellis: That's fine. What was the idea behind it? What did you want to do differently?

[00:01:54] Amrit Sandhu: The honest version is that I was tired of clinics that were like factories. You know the kind, three patients an hour and the physio hooks you up to a machine and leaves. I wanted one-on-one time, real assessments, and a lot of exercise-based care. It's a bit of a cliché now because everybody says it, but in 2009 in Calgary it really set us apart. And I wanted a place where young physios would actually learn something.

[00:02:17] Morgan Ellis: And the move to the current Hillhurst space?

[00:02:20] Amrit Sandhu: June 2017. We'd completely outgrown the first place. We were booking treatment rooms in fifteen-minute slots and still turning people away. The Wexford Avenue space is 3,800 square feet. We have ten treatment spaces, six private rooms plus an open gym with four plinths, three massage rooms, and a Pilates studio with two reformers. It was a big step up.

[00:02:43] Morgan Ellis: And Seton came in 2021.

[00:02:46] Amrit Sandhu: September 2021, yes. It was a bit crazy to open during COVID, but the lease terms were good because landlords were nervous. We got a tenant allowance, three months of free fixturing and an exclusive, so they can't put another physio clinic in the development. The southeast was booming, it still is, and a lot of our Hillhurst patients were driving forty minutes from Auburn Bay and Mahogany. So we followed them.

[00:03:10] Morgan Ellis: Let's come back to Seton in a minute. Give me the business in one breath. What are you, today?

[00:03:17] Amrit Sandhu: Two clinics, Hillhurst in the northwest and Seton in the southeast. Eleven physios including me, six massage therapists, and five people in admin, counting Dana and Harjit. We do physiotherapy, registered massage, clinical Pilates and exercise classes, and we sell some braces and orthotics. About three point three million in revenue in 2024. And 2025 was better. I think we'll land around three forty-five or three forty-six once Ridgeline finishes.

[00:03:43] Morgan Ellis: Is that from your internal books?

[00:03:45] Amrit Sandhu: Yes, from ClinicNest and Harjit's ledger. Dana could give you it by month. I'd say Hillhurst was up again and Seton was back over eight hundred thousand. I'll let her give you the exact numbers. I'd hate to be off by fifty grand on a recorded call.

[00:04:00] Morgan Ellis: Wise. On earnings, when we first spoke in December you said around seven hundred of seller's discretionary earnings. For 2024 I get six ninety from the statements: EBITDA of about four twenty-six, plus your salary, plus the normal add-backs. Does that match how you see it?

[00:04:18] Amrit Sandhu: That's about right. Ridgeline showed me something very close. I'd guess 2025 comes in around seven twenty. But again, I'm guessing.

[00:04:28] Morgan Ellis: Good. Let's go through the add-backs so there are no surprises. Your salary is one-eighty. Harjit's wages, your vehicle, some personal travel, the legal fees for rewriting the agreements, and the Seton flood.

[00:04:42] Amrit Sandhu: Right. The flood was March 2024. A pipe burst in the unit above and took out the flooring in two treatment rooms. Insurance covered most of it, but we paid the deductible and some flooring they wouldn't cover. So yes, that's one-time. The legal fees were Chinook redoing all the contractor agreements in the spring of 2024. The old 2019 form was thin, and, well, we found out exactly how thin.

[00:05:02] Morgan Ellis: You mean Ethan Marsh?

[00:05:05] Amrit Sandhu: (pause) Yes. Ethan was an associate at Seton. Good physio. When we rolled out the new agreement in March he kept putting off signing it, and in hindsight I know why. He cut back to three days that spring, left at the end of October 2024 and opened his own place in Auburn Bay, about three kilometres from Seton. He was still on the old 2019 agreement, which had a non-solicit but no radius clause. So legally he could do it.

[00:31:28] Morgan Ellis: It's a plan, not a promise. If the 2025 compilation slips, everything moves.

[00:31:33] Amrit Sandhu: I'll push Paul.

[00:31:35] Morgan Ellis: (laughs) Please. One more thing on the numbers. The 2025 internal figures, three forty-six and around seven twenty of SDE. I'll call those unaudited management estimates until Ridgeline finishes. I won't put a firm 2025 number in the CIM until the compilation is done.

[00:31:50] Amrit Sandhu: That's fair. I'd rather under-promise.

[00:31:53] Morgan Ellis: Good. Anything else from your side?

[00:31:56] Amrit Sandhu: Just a question. Will buyers talk to the staff before closing?

[00:32:00] Morgan Ellis: Only at the very end, and only the key people, usually Leah, Dana and Marcus, and only with your agreement. It usually happens after the LOI, in the last few weeks of due diligence.

[00:32:10] Amrit Sandhu: Okay. That makes me feel better.

[00:32:13] Amrit Sandhu: Actually, since I have a few more minutes, can I ask how buyers will value this? Harjit keeps asking me what "three and a half times" means.

[00:32:21] Morgan Ellis: Sure. Most buyers for a clinic your size start from seller's discretionary earnings, the six ninety, or from an adjusted EBITDA where they take out a market salary for someone to replace your management role. For you that's probably a clinic director at around one-fifty with benefits, which gets you to about five-forty of adjusted EBITDA. Two point four is about three and a half times SDE, or about four and a half times adjusted EBITDA. That's a reasonable range for a two-location clinic with your history.

[00:32:52] Amrit Sandhu: And the consolidators look at EBITDA?

[00:32:55] Morgan Ellis: Almost always. They'll also look at your clinical billings. You personally bill about one forty-six a year. When you step back, that revenue either goes away or an associate takes it on at a sixty-five percent split. So they'll adjust for that as well.

[00:33:10] Amrit Sandhu: That's why staying two days a week matters.

[00:33:13] Morgan Ellis: Exactly. It protects that revenue while your patients move to other physios. The other thing buyers look at is working capital. You run lean. Receivables are about two-fifteen, mostly insurers and the MVA claims, and on the other side are the practitioner fees payable and normal payables. Net working capital is only about fifty-five thousand. We'll agree on a normal level that stays with the business, and you keep the cash above that.

[00:33:40] Amrit Sandhu: So the cash in the bank is mine?

[00:33:42] Morgan Ellis: In a cash-free, debt-free deal, generally yes, after the bank loan is paid out. On a share sale, Paul will want to plan the timing around dividends too. That's for him and your lawyer.

[00:33:54] Amrit Sandhu: Right. Paul has opinions. (laughs)

[00:33:57] Morgan Ellis: Good accountants do. Then there's the data room. After the NDA, serious buyers get access to a secure folder with the statements, the leases, the roster and so on. Cimple tracks who looks at what, so we know who's serious before we spend time with them.

[00:34:12] Amrit Sandhu: Can they download everything?

[00:34:14] Morgan Ellis: We control that. Early on it's view-only and watermarked. Patient information never goes in, obviously. Anything about staff pay is summarized until late in the process.

[00:34:24] Amrit Sandhu: Good. The associates would be upset if a buyer saw their splits before they knew there was a buyer.

[00:34:30] Morgan Ellis: Agreed. Let me ask about the MVA claims one more time, since buyers will ask. The eighteen thousand in dispute. Is it one insurer?

[00:34:38] Amrit Sandhu: One insurer, two patients. Both were rear-end collisions. The insurer says the treatment went past the protocol limits without pre-approval, and Dana says we had the approvals. It'll probably settle at part of that. I wouldn't count on all of it.

[00:34:52] Morgan Ellis: We'll show it as a possible reserve rather than hide it. Okay. Last one from me, the equipment. Are the ultrasound units old?

[00:35:00] Amrit Sandhu: Some are from 2017, some newer. They're simple machines. Honestly, the modern approach is more hands-on and exercise, so we use them less every year. The reformers are 2023, and the shockwave is 2024. The computers were refreshed in 2024.

[00:35:14] Morgan Ellis: So a buyer isn't walking into a big capital bill.

[00:35:17] Amrit Sandhu: No. The biggest one would be finishing that Hillhurst storage room, maybe forty to fifty thousand for two treatment rooms. Plinths over the next few years. And if someone wants a third clinic, that's a real build-out. Seton cost about three-forty all in, build-out and equipment, before the landlord's allowance.

[00:35:34] Morgan Ellis: Three-forty for Seton, before the allowance?

[00:35:37] Amrit Sandhu: Around there before the seventy-eight thousand allowance. The bank loan covered the rest, plus the opening costs while it ramped up. I'd have to check the exact number with Harjit.

[00:35:45] Morgan Ellis: That's useful context for anyone thinking about a third location. Okay, I think that's plenty for today. It was very helpful. I'll send a summary and the interview link this week.

[00:35:55] Amrit Sandhu: Thanks, Morgan. Sorry for the rambling.

[00:35:58] Morgan Ellis: Not at all. That's what I needed. The stories are what make the CIM.

[00:36:03] Amrit Sandhu: Oh, before you go. The team day in June. If the sale is happening around then, I'd like to keep it. It matters to people.

[00:36:11] Morgan Ellis: I don't see why not. Any buyer would be foolish to cancel it.

[00:36:15] Amrit Sandhu: (laughs) Put that in the CIM. "Buyer must attend team barbecue."

[00:36:20] Morgan Ellis: I'll leave that for the closing agreement. (laughs) Have a good clinic day, Amrit.

[00:36:24] Amrit Sandhu: You too. Bye.

[00:36:26] -- Amrit Sandhu left the meeting --

[00:36:40] Morgan Ellis: (voice memo while recording, for file) Clearwater follow-ups. One: Seton framing. Present contribution first, then the allocated view. He says it "breaks even" and he's firm on that, but Dana's report shows about minus twenty-four after overhead. Ask the interview to probe it and get Dana's 2025 location P&L. Two: how many patients followed Ethan Marsh. He was vague and said "a handful." Three: retention for Leah and Dana. Leah turned down Bowmont last fall and got a raise to one twenty-four. Four: the Greg Tallis email about the storage room expansion. Five: the Hillhurst landlord strategy waits until after the LOI, and the renewal window is August 31 to November 30.
