messages.content: One area I'd like to fill in: how would you describe Clearwater's reputation in the Calgary physio market, and what do you think sets it apart from competitors like Bowmont or other multi-location chains?

You know, honestly I think we've built something pretty different from the Bowmont model. They're volume-driven – 15-minute follow-ups, a lot of turnover, very corporate. We're the opposite. Every follow-up is 45 minutes, one-on-one. People notice that. I had a patient last year tell me her daughter saw someone at a Bowmont clinic and felt like she was on a conveyor belt. That's not us.

Our reputation in Hillhurst especially is rock-solid – we've been in the community since 2009, and I've treated three generations of one family. The Bhatias: grandmother came in 2011 with a frozen shoulder, her son tore his ACL playing soccer in 2016, and now the grandson's in our concussion program after a hockey hit. That's the kind of trust you can't buy.

The reviews speak for themselves – 4.8 stars on about 900 reviews. People mention the time we take, the fact that they see the same clinician, and the range of what we offer under one roof. Concussion and vestibular work, pelvic health with Kelsey, clinical Pilates, shockwave – most independent clinics don't have all of that. The chains have scale, but we have depth and continuity. And our team has stayed. Leah's been with me since 2014, Aimee the RMT since 2011, Dana since 2012. That stability shows.

Seton's newer, so we're still building that same depth there, but the exclusive-use clause in that development helps.
What's the typical path a new patient takes to find Clearwater — is it mainly word of mouth and physician referrals, or does online search and marketing play a meaningful role?

Honestly, it's shifted a lot over the years. When I opened in 2009, it was almost all physician referrals and word of mouth. Now I'd say online search is probably the biggest single channel – maybe 40% of new patients find us that way. They Google "physio near me" or "concussion clinic Calgary," they see the reviews, they book through the website. We're on the first page for a bunch of local searches, and the 4.8-star rating does the heavy lifting.

Word of mouth and returning patients are still strong – maybe 30%. People tell their friends, or they come back themselves for something new. I've had patients I first saw for a back issue in 2012 come back for pelvic health or send their kids to us for sports injuries.

The other 30% is a mix. We get referrals from two family-practice groups near Hillhurst – they know us, they trust the quality. There's a spine surgeon's office that sends post-op patients our way. And Leah built the concussion program, so we get referrals from the Glenmore Ironhawks junior A team and a few high-school athletic departments. WCB and the MVA insurers send people directly sometimes, too.

We don't do a ton of paid marketing anymore – maybe $4,000 a month across both clinics, mostly Google Ads and a bit of Facebook. The reputation does a lot of the work now. Seton's still building that organic referral base, so we skew a bit heavier on ads there.

Are those physician referral relationships — the two family-practice groups near Hillhurst and the spine surgeon — with the clinic formally, or are they more personal relationships you've built that would need to be handed off to a new owner?

That's a good question, and honestly... it's more the latter. They're personal relationships I've built over the years. The two family docs — one of them, Dr. Patel, I met through a mutual patient back in 2011, and we just started referring back and forth. The other group, I can't even remember how it started, but I've been getting their referrals for probably a decade. The spine surgeon, Dr. Kowalski, I know from some continuing-ed courses we both taught at. He trusts me with his post-op cases because he knows how I work.

So yeah, they're tied to me personally, not formally to the clinic. There's no contract or anything like that. A new owner would need to build their own relationships, or I'd need to make introductions during the transition. I think if I stay on for a while and we do a proper handoff — "this is the new clinical director, they're excellent, I'm staying involved" — most of that would transfer. But I'm not going to pretend it's automatic.

That said, the online piece and the word-of-mouth piece aren't tied to me. And even the physician referrals — a lot of them now come to Leah or Priya directly, not me. Leah especially with the concussion work. So it's not like I'm the only referral magnet. But I'd be lying if I said my name doesn't open some doors, you know?

That's a realistic read — and the fact that Leah and Priya already receive direct referrals helps. On the topic of your team's forward plans: have any of your physiotherapists or RMTs indicated they're thinking about leaving, retiring, or cutting back their hours in the next year or two?

No, knock on wood. The PT and RMT group is pretty stable right now. Nobody's told me they're planning to leave or cut back. Leah just got the raise in October after Bowmont tried to poach her, so she's locked in. Marcus at Seton wants *more* responsibility, not less. Priya's been with me since 2016 and she's at her peak earning years. The associates all seem happy with their caseloads.

The RMTs are all independent contractors, so they come and go as they please, but the longest-tenured ones — Aimee, Grant, Mei-Lin — have been around for years and I haven't heard any rumblings.

The one person I *do* worry about medium-term is Dana. She's 58, and she's mentioned a few times that she's thinking about retiring in maybe three years. Not imminent, but it's on her radar. She's the institutional knowledge — scheduling, billing, payer protocols, all of it. Replacing her is going to take some real planning. I'd want to overlap someone with her for at least six months, maybe a year, to transfer everything.

Harjit's leaving at closing, obviously, but that's by design. The bookkeeping piece is straightforward to replace — Dana says we can get someone for $20-25k a year to do what Harjit does.

So short answer: the clinical team is solid. Dana's the succession risk, but we've got a bit of runway there.
On the patient acquisition side — roughly what does it cost you to acquire a new patient through paid channels like Google Ads, and do you track that?

Honestly, I don't track it as closely as I probably should. Dana pulls some reports from Google Ads every quarter, but we've never really nailed down a true cost-per-acquisition number. It's one of those things where I know we spend about $4,000 a month on marketing — call it $50k a year — and we brought in roughly 2,150 new patients in FY2024, so back-of-the-envelope that's maybe $23 per new patient across all channels. But that includes the organic search, word of mouth, all of it, not just the paid ads.

If I had to guess on *just* the paid piece... maybe we're getting 30-40% of new patients from Google Ads? So call it 650-850 new patients from ads, which would put the cost somewhere in the $60-75 range per new patient from paid search. But that's a rough guess, you know? Dana would have better numbers from the ad account, and honestly a new owner with better analytics could probably get that cost down. We're not optimizing it the way a marketing person would.

What I *do* know is that the lifetime value is strong. A new patient who comes in for physio usually stays for 6-8 visits on average, sometimes way more if it's a chronic issue, and a lot of them come back later or refer someone. So even at $75 to acquire them, it pencils out pretty well.

Amrit, we've covered a lot of ground — your market position, referral channels, team stability, and customer acquisition. We have strong documentation on the financials, leases, and operations already. Is there anything you feel buyers should know that we haven't touched on, or shall we wrap up for today?

You know, I think we've covered the mechanics pretty well. If I had to add one thing buyers should understand... it's that this business runs on trust and continuity, not flash. We're not the biggest, we're not the cheapest, we don't have the fanciest equipment. What we have is a team that shows up, patients who feel cared for, and a reputation we've earned one appointment at a time over 16 years.

The numbers are solid — you've got all of that — but the *reason* the numbers are solid is because people come back and they tell their friends. That doesn't happen by accident. It happens because Leah spends an extra ten minutes explaining a vestibular exercise, or because Dana remembers a patient's name and asks how their kid's doing, or because we don't rush people out the door.

So whoever buys this... I hope they get that. The model works *because* it's relationship-driven. You can't strip-mine it. If someone comes in thinking they're going to cut follow-ups to 30 minutes and double-book to squeeze more revenue, they'll kill the thing that makes it valuable.

I want to sell to someone who's going to keep building what we've started — fill Seton, maybe add that third location, bring Dana's replacement up to speed, keep Leah happy. I'll help with all of that. I'm not trying to dump this and disappear. I want to stay involved clinically and see it thrive.

That's probably the most important thing I haven't said yet. Does that make sense?

That makes complete sense, and it's exactly the kind of insight that helps the right buyer understand what they're stepping into. The relationship-driven model is the asset — and your willingness to stay involved clinically gives a buyer real continuity to build on.

We've covered the core ground today. There are a few operational items your broker will follow up on separately — things like confirming there are no College complaints on file, WCB audit history, and how the direct billing credentials transfer in a share sale. Dana would know most of that.

Thanks for your time, Amrit. This gives us a strong foundation for the CIM.

Welcome back, Amrit. One question that came up as I was reviewing: has the clinic ever had any complaints filed with the Alberta College of Physiotherapists or CRMTA against any of the practitioners — resolved or otherwise?

Good question. There was one College complaint back in 2023 — it was against one of the associates, not me. A patient felt they weren't progressing fast enough and filed a complaint alleging the PT wasn't adjusting the treatment plan appropriately. The College investigated, reviewed the chart notes, and dismissed it with no finding. No disciplinary action, nothing on the public register. The associate handled it well, stayed professional throughout.

That's the only one I'm aware of in the entire history of the clinic. No complaints against me, none against the RMTs with CRMTA. We've been pretty fortunate that way, honestly. I think part of it is the time we spend with patients — when people feel heard and they understand what's happening, they're less likely to escalate frustrations into formal complaints.

Dana keeps a file on it — the College's closure letter and the associate's response documentation — so that's available if a buyer wants to see it. But yeah, one complaint in 16 years, dismissed. That's the full story there.

Anything else on compliance you want to dig into?
Has the clinic ever been audited by WCB-Alberta on its billing practices?

Yeah, we had one audit — it was back in 2019, I think. Maybe early 2020, right before COVID. It was a routine random audit, not triggered by anything specific. They pulled a sample of maybe 30 or 40 WCB claims from the previous year, reviewed the chart notes, checked that the billing codes matched the documentation and the treatment provided.

They found a couple of minor discrepancies — I think one was a billing code that should have been stepped down because the session ran short, and maybe one or two notes that could have been more detailed on the functional outcomes. Nothing fraudulent, just documentation tightening. They asked us to refund maybe $400 or $500, which we did immediately, and Dana put in some extra chart-review checks after that to make sure we were dotting every i.

No penalties, no further follow-up, and we haven't been audited since. WCB payments have been smooth ever since — they pay pretty reliably, usually within 30-40 days.

Dana would have the audit letter and our response if you need it, but honestly it was about as clean as those things get. I know some clinics that have had way messier WCB audits. We were lucky, and Dana's diligent about the documentation rules.
When was the last IPAC inspection at either location, and were there any findings?

Honestly, I'd have to check with Dana on the exact dates. IPAC — Infection Prevention and Control — those inspections happen through AHS, and they're not on a super regular schedule for outpatient clinics like ours. I think the last one at Hillhurst was maybe 2022 or early 2023? And Seton might have had one right after we opened in 2021 as part of the initial approval process.

From what I remember, both were clean. They check things like hand hygiene, how we're storing and disinfecting equipment, laundry handling for linens, sharps disposal for the dry needling. We've always been pretty tight on that stuff — Dana makes sure the protocols are posted and the staff are trained. I don't recall any findings or corrective actions from the last inspections.

But Dana keeps all the IPAC documentation and inspection reports in the compliance binder, so she can pull the actual dates and any letters if you need them. I just don't have that level of detail off the top of my head. Is that something the broker's checklist is asking for specifically?
One more compliance question: does the clinic sell any prepaid treatment packages or memberships where patients pay upfront for multiple visits?

No, we don't. We bill per visit. Some clinics do those packages — you know, "buy 10 sessions, get a discount" — but we've never gone that route. Partly it's because most of our patients are using insurance or WCB or MVA, so they're not paying out of pocket anyway. And for the private-pay patients, I've never loved the optics of locking someone into a package when we don't know how many sessions they'll actually need. It feels a bit... I don't know, salesy? That's not our style.

The one exception is the Pilates classes. We sell class packs — like a 10-class pass for reformer Pilates at a slight discount versus drop-in. But those are handled as deferred revenue on the books. When someone buys a 10-class pack, the revenue gets recognized as they use the classes, not all upfront. The accountant makes sure that's done properly. I think at any given time we might have $8,000 to $12,000 in unused class-pack credits on the books, but Dana tracks that in ClinicNest and it's reflected in the financials.

So short answer: no prepaid physio or massage packages, just the Pilates class packs, and those are accounted for correctly as deferred revenue. Does that answer what you're after?

On the direct billing side — you're enrolled with five major insurers. In a share sale, do those direct billing credentials transfer automatically to the new owner, or is there a re-enrollment process?

That's a really good question, and honestly I'm not 100% certain on the mechanics. My understanding is that in a share sale, because the corporation stays the same — same name, same business number — the billing agreements *should* transfer automatically. The company is still Clearwater Physiotherapy & Wellness Inc., just with a different shareholder. But I don't know if the insurers have notification requirements or if they need to re-credential the new owner as the clinical director.

Dana would know this better than me — she set up all the direct billing agreements and deals with the insurers constantly. My gut says Prairie Shield, Northgate, Maplecrest, all of them... they're billing the *company*, not me personally. But if the new owner isn't a licensed PT, that might be an issue. I don't know if they require the owner to be a practicing clinician or if they just care that the practitioners treating patients are licensed.

This is definitely something the buyer's lawyer and Dana should confirm with each insurer before closing. The last thing you want is a gap in direct billing capability while you're waiting for re-enrollment. That would be a mess.

I can ask Dana to pull the agreements and flag any change-of-control clauses, if that helps? Or the broker can reach out to her directly on this one. It's a detail I should have nailed down already, to be honest.

That's exactly right — your broker will want Dana to pull those insurer agreements and check for any change-of-control language before marketing. The mechanics vary by insurer, and buyers will want certainty that direct billing continues without interruption.

On patient records: in a share sale, the records stay with the corporation. But does ClinicNest have a standard process for ownership transfers, or would there be any data migration involved?

ClinicNest is cloud-based, so the records themselves don't physically move anywhere — they're already in the system. In a share sale, yeah, the corporation owns the account and all the data, so technically it just continues as-is. The new owner would get admin access, we'd remove my login and Harjit's, add theirs, and it keeps running.

That said, I think ClinicNest has a formal ownership-transfer process we'd need to follow. They probably want documentation — share purchase agreement, proof of new ownership, maybe a privacy impact assessment because we're dealing with personal health information under Alberta's HIA. I've never done it, so I don't know exactly what they require, but I know other clinics that have sold, and the practice management system transfer is usually pretty straightforward as long as you give them notice and the right paperwork.

Dana's our ClinicNest admin, so she'd coordinate that with their support team. I think we'd want to do it *after* closing but have it teed up in advance so there's no downtime. Patients book online through ClinicNest, so if the system went dark for even a day, that would be a problem.

The good news is there's no data migration — we're not moving from one system to another. It's just a change of ownership within the same ClinicNest account. But yeah, we should confirm the process with them ahead of time. I can have Dana reach out to ClinicNest and ask what they need for an ownership transfer, if that's helpful?
One more on this front: who actually owns the patient records — the clinic corporation, or do individual practitioners retain any ownership of charts for patients they treat?

The corporation owns all the patient records — that's explicit in our associate agreements and it's been that way since we incorporated. When a practitioner joins, they acknowledge that any clinical notes they create in ClinicNest belong to Clearwater Physiotherapy & Wellness Inc. We're the custodian under Alberta's HIA, and honestly it has to be that way for continuity of care and our direct-billing obligations. If someone leaves, they don't take charts with them, though we'll forward records to another clinic if a patient requests it in writing. Right now we've got about 3,900 active patient charts in the system.
Shifting to the team structure: of your 11 physiotherapists, how many are T4 employees versus independent contractors?

Sorry, I misspoke a second ago: it's about 4,300 active patient charts, not 3,900. On the PTs, honestly I think you already have that from the roster: three of us are on T4, me, Leah and Marcus, and the other eight are associates on contractor agreements.
And the six RMTs — are they all on signed contractor agreements, or are any on the older 2019 form like Hannah?

All six RMTs are on the same 2022 contractor agreement, all signed, none on the old form. And just so you understand why I want to drop to two days a week after the sale: my dad was diagnosed with Parkinson's last year and I'm helping my mom with his care, but keep that out of the book please.

That goes to your broker only, never the sale document.

Beyond Ethan Marsh leaving last October, have any other PTs or RMTs left in the past three years?
Just Ethan, really, plus one RMT who moved to Edmonton in 2023 for family reasons. Sorry, I have to run, I've got a patient in five minutes. Can we pick this up tomorrow?

Of course — we've covered a lot of ground. Before you go, the one thing I'd most like to confirm is whether both clinic premises are zoned for healthcare or therapy use. A quick yes now, or shall we start there next time?
Let's start there next time, I really have to go now.
Absolutely — we'll pick up with the zoning question next time. Everything's saved, and your broker will follow up with Dana on the insurer agreements and IPAC documentation. Talk soon.

greatLakes.text: Good to pick up where we left off, Diane — last time we got into the tool room, press fleet, and your medical pipeline. You mentioned replacing the older hydraulics two or three at a time — what's the annual budget you're planning for that press replacement program, and how many years until the fleet is where you want it?

We've been running about $3 million total capex the last couple years, and figure $1.6 million of that is just maintenance — keeping the lights on. The rest goes to growth equipment or these press swaps. If we replace two or three of the old hydraulics a year, that's probably $600,000 to $900,000 depending on tonnage, so call it three to four more years to get the ten oldest machines out. Rob's got the list by age, but honestly a buyer with better access to capital could accelerate that — we're doing it as cash flow allows, and the personal guarantees make me cautious about adding more term debt.
How is your workforce structured across the three shifts — roughly how many people on each, and are any shifts harder to staff than others?

First shift runs about 85 people, second around 75, third maybe 50 plus the temps scattered across all three. Third is always the hardest — that $2-an-hour premium helps, but turnover on nights is closer to 40% versus maybe 25% on days. Luis, our plant manager, has been juggling it for years; we've had better luck since we started hiring through Quillon for temp-to-perm on third, gives people a trial run before they commit to midnights. Skilled positions — setup techs, toolmakers — those are all first shift, which is another reason third is lean.

Quick clarification before we move on: the org chart shows 112 setup and process technicians across the three shifts, but you mentioned the skilled positions are concentrated on first shift. Are those 112 the operators themselves, or is that a separate count of your setup techs?

No, you're reading it wrong — the 112 is press operators and packers, the people running the machines and boxing parts. The setup and process technicians are a separate line, 22 of them. Most of those 22 are on first shift, maybe four or five on second, one or two floaters on third who can handle basic adjustments. The operators don't change molds or dial in a new program; the techs do that. Sorry if the chart wasn't clear — Tom put it together and sometimes the labels run together.
The org chart Tom put together didn't specify a count for that line. Is 22 the current headcount, or is that an approximation?

That's the current headcount — 22 setup and process techs. I just pulled it from the payroll summary Tom gave me last week when we were getting ready for this round of calls. If you need the exact breakdown by shift I can get that from Luis, but 22 is the right number as of end of May.
On the equipment liens — I see the term loans are secured by equipment and get paid off at closing. Are those liens on specific presses, or is it a blanket lien across the whole fleet?

Blanket lien on all the equipment with First Maumee — they financed the 2023 and 2024 press buys plus some ancillary stuff, and they just took a general security interest in machinery and equipment. It's not press-by-press. The payoff's about $5.1 million as of the end of March, and yeah, that all gets cleared at closing so the buyer gets everything free and clear. Tom has the exact payoff letter if you need it, but it's straightforward — no carve-outs, no weird subordination.
On the company-owned molds — the 15 to 18 you mentioned last time — are those included in the sale, or would they stay with the family?

They're included. Those are production molds we built for parts we sell to smaller customers or for samples and prototypes. They're assets of the business, not personal property, so they transfer with everything else. The customer-owned tooling obviously stays with the customers — we're just the custodian — but our molds go with the sale.

When Diane and Rob's non-compete period ends after the sale — two years, per the shareholders' agreement — are there any geographic or industry restrictions built into that, or is it a blanket prohibition on injection molding work?

You're mixing things up. The shareholders' agreement has a non-compete that runs while you're a shareholder and for two years after you leave — that's to keep one of us from jumping ship and opening a shop across town while we still own the company together. At closing we're all out, so that agreement terminates. The buyer will want a new non-compete as part of the purchase agreement — I'll sign whatever's standard, probably three to five years, and I'd expect it to cover the Great Lakes region and our end markets, automotive and medical molding. Rob will do the same if he's staying on under an employment deal. But the old shareholders' agreement covenant isn't what governs after the sale.

On a related item: Diane and Rob have personally guaranteed the bank debt with First Maumee. What's your expectation for how those guarantees get handled at closing — full release, or would the bank require anything from the buyer?

Full release at closing — the debt gets paid off, the guarantees die with it. That's one of the big reasons I want to sell, frankly; I'm tired of having the house on the line every time we finance a press. The buyer will put their own capital structure in place, and First Maumee is out of the picture. If the buyer wants to keep banking with them that's their business, but our guarantees are gone the day the wire hits.
Has First Maumee confirmed in writing that payoff at closing fully releases the personal guarantees, or is that still a conversation your attorney needs to button up?

Tom got a payoff-and-release letter from them back in March when we told them we were exploring a sale — it says payment in full releases all guarantees and liens. Our attorney, Julie Hendricks, reviewed it and said it's standard. So yes, it's in writing and buttoned up.

Shifting to the working capital side: I see year-end working capital running around $6.5 to $6.8 million. Does that stay relatively flat through the year, or does it swing meaningfully with the automotive production schedule?

It swings — spring is the peak, March through May, when the Tier-1s are building for summer and we're carrying more AR and inventory. We might be up to $7.2 or $7.5 million in April. Then it comes down over the summer, especially during the July shutdown, and sits around $6 million in the fall. The peg will probably land somewhere in the middle, $6.5 to $6.8 million trailing-twelve average, but Tom will give you the month-by-month if you want to see the curve.
How does your working capital peg get calculated in a typical deal — are you expecting it to be based on a trailing-twelve-month average, or a point-in-time snapshot at closing?

Trailing-twelve average is what I've been told is normal for a company our size with seasonality, and that's what I just said — $6.5 to $6.8 million. You set the peg in the LOI based on that average, then at closing you true it up to what's actually on the books that day. If we deliver more working capital than the peg, the buyer pays us the difference; if we're under, we write them a check. Tom's done it before on a smaller deal years ago, so he knows the drill. Does that match what you're expecting?

One last detail: on the working capital swings you mentioned — $7.2 to $7.5 million in spring, down to around $6 million in fall — is that driven more by receivables timing from the Tier-1s, or by raw material and finished goods inventory builds?

Both, but inventory is the bigger driver. We build ahead in March and April because the Tier-1s give us firm releases and they hate line-downs, so we're carrying an extra two or three weeks of safety stock. Receivables stretch a little — Maumee Valley and Lakeshore pay in 45 to 50 days — but that's pretty steady year-round. The real swing is resin and finished goods. Then in July everything ships out before the shutdown and we run inventory down, and AR collects while we're dark, so cash peaks and working capital drops. It's a nice little cycle once you get used to it.

We've covered a lot of ground today — shift structure, equipment liens, the guarantees, non-compete terms, and how working capital moves through the year. The one area still open from earlier is the exact tooling list Rob keeps — if he can send that over to Morgan, it would fill in the last piece on mold ownership.

lakeshore.text: Good to pick up where we left off — we covered a lot of ground on the licensing, Comfort Club, and your key people last time. One thing I wanted to ask about: your financials show $378,000 in vehicle expenses in 2024, which is on the higher side relative to revenue — is that driven by the fleet age, fuel costs, or something else a buyer should understand?

Yeah, listen, it's a combination. Fuel's a big part — we put serious kilometres on those trucks, you know what I mean? Twenty-four vans running all over Hamilton, Burlington, out to Oakville sometimes, that adds up fast. Plus insurance went up again last year, maintenance on some of the older units — we've got seven vans that are 2018 or older, a couple of the plumbing vans are 2016, so they need more love. We budget three, four vans a year for replacement at around sixty-eight grand upfitted, but honestly the older ones, you're into brakes, transmissions, that kind of thing. It's not out of line for a fleet this size, but yeah, a buyer's gonna want to keep cycling those older ones out.

Now, before we keep going — I want to know what Morgan's actually using for the add-backs and what SDE number did she come up with for 2024? Because I've got my own ideas, but I want to see what you guys are working with. What's the actual number?

The SDE calculation is something Morgan finalizes directly with the financials — I don't have her working number to share, and honestly that's the right conversation to have with her since she's the one who'll defend it to buyers. What I can help with is making sure we've captured the items that typically get considered. From what's on file: your $240K management salary, Maria's $85K, the $38K in vehicle loan interest, and the $214K in amortization. Are there other expenses in 2024 that were one-time or discretionary — things that wouldn't recur for a new owner?

Okay, fair enough — yeah, I'll nail that down with Morgan. But listen, you're missing stuff. The twenty-eight thousand in owner vehicles — my RAM and Maria's Lexus lease, that's personal, that comes out. The health and life insurance premiums for me and Maria, that's another nine grand. Meals and entertainment, honestly half of that is me taking suppliers out or the Tiger-Cats box, call it eleven thousand discretionary. 

And here's a big one you didn't mention — we had a former employee, wrongful dismissal thing, settled it in July, cost us twenty-two thousand in legal fees that's buried in professional fees. That's one-time, that's gone, that should absolutely be an add-back.

So you've got the salaries, the vehicles, the insurance, the meals, the legal — that's way more than just amortization and interest. Denise has all this broken out, she gave it to Morgan. Are you guys not working off the same sheet here?

You're right — those items are in the documents Denise sent, I should have had them in front of me. I'll make sure the owner vehicles ($28K), health and life insurance ($9K), discretionary meals ($11K).

One quick item while we're on housekeeping: the financials show a $60,000 due to shareholder that's been sitting there with no fixed repayment terms. Your broker will confirm what gets added back when they normalize the numbers against your statements. Is that something you'd expect to settle at closing, or would it stay on the books for the buyer to assume?

Whoa, hold on — that sixty thousand, that's mine, that's money I lent the company years ago when we moved into the new building, you know what I mean? That gets paid out to me at closing, no question. The buyer's not assuming that, that's not their debt, that's owed to me personally.

Listen, the deal is cash-free, debt-free — we pay out the vehicle loans or the buyer assumes them at a credit to the price, and I take my sixty grand. Clean balance sheet. That's how Morgan explained it to me and that's what I agreed to.

Honestly, I don't want any of this nickel-and-dime stuff scaring off a buyer — the business clears about a million and a half when you add everything back, we've got twenty-six trucks on the road, twenty-nine hundred members paying every month, and I'm here for six months full-time to make sure it goes smooth. At the end of the day, that's what matters, right?

One quick clarification: you mentioned twenty-six trucks on the road, but the fleet list Denise sent shows 24 service vans plus your two personal vehicles that are excluded from the sale. Which number is right — are there 24 or 26 service vans actually running routes?

Twenty-four, you're right — twenty-four service vans. I round up in my head sometimes, you know what I mean? We've got the two plumbing vans, twenty-two HVAC, that's twenty-four on the road every day. My RAM and Maria's Lexus don't count, those are ours. 

Listen, Denise's list is the gospel on that stuff — if she says twenty-four, it's twenty-four. I'm out there running the business, not counting trucks in the yard every morning.
Switching gears — the staff roster lists your technicians' licences, but I want to make sure we capture the 313A refrigeration certifications specifically. How many of your techs hold the 313A?

We've got six guys with the 313A — that's your refrigeration, your A/C work. Denise has it all broken down on the licensing summary she sent you, but yeah, six 313A, eleven with the 313D gas, five plumbers with the 306A. Some of the guys have multiples — like Dave and Kevin and Luis all have both the A and the D.

Honestly we could use one or two more 313A guys — heat pump installs, you need the refrigeration ticket for the line sets and the charging, you know what I mean? Hard to find good people with that ticket right now.

You mentioned it's hard to find 313A techs right now — have any of your licensed guys given you any indication they might leave, or is there anyone beyond Dave and Sal you'd flag as a flight risk if the ownership changes?

Nobody's said a word about leaving. Dave's the one I'd watch, honestly, he's hinted he wants a piece of it. Sal's been with me sixteen years, he's not going anywhere. But listen, at the end of the day this business clears about a million and a half a year, you know what I mean? Is that the number going in the book?

Quick clarification: the staff roster shows Sal starting in 2009, which would be about sixteen years — so that tracks. On the retention question for the other licensed techs beyond Dave and Sal: is there anything you'd put in place to keep them through a transition — any retention bonuses or commitments you'd expect a buyer to offer?

Listen, I already answered the retention thing — nobody's said they're leaving, Dave wants in, Sal's solid, the Fernandes brothers have been here forever. You give them a heads-up, you treat them right, they'll stay. Maybe a buyer throws Dave a little equity or a bump, but I'm not gonna start handing out retention bonuses for guys who aren't going anywhere.

Now seriously — you keep dodging my question. The business clears about a million and a half when you add everything back. Is that the SDE number Morgan's putting in the book or not? Because if we're gonna list this thing at four-eight, I need to know what multiple she's using and what she's telling buyers the cash flow is. You're the one building the book, right? So what's the number?

Let me ask about something else on the licensing side: besides you and Dave as the G1 certificate holders on the TSSA registration, who are the other master licence holders across the business — anyone else whose name appears on a company registration or who holds a licence the business operates under?

It's just me and Dave on the TSSA contractor registration — that's the G1 gas. That's the one that matters for the company to operate. Kevin's got his G2, Sal's got his G2, but they're not certificate holders on the company registration, you know what I mean? They work under our umbrella.

We don't have an electrical contractor licence — that's why we sub out the panel work to Voltmere. And the plumbing, there's no master plumber registration in Ontario like some provinces, it's all individual tickets. Sal's the lead guy, he's got his 306A, but there's no company plumbing licence with his name on it.

So bottom line: me and Dave on the TSSA, that's it. And Dave stays, so the buyer just needs to get their own G1 or bring someone in, and we update the certificate holders with TSSA. It's straightforward.

Now are you gonna tell me what SDE Morgan's using or do I need to call her after this?

One thing that would help round out the employee section: the staff roster shows certifications, but for the CIM I'd like to list out which specific technicians hold which licences. Could Denise send over a breakdown showing each tech's name alongside their certifications — the 313A, 313D, and 306A holders individually?

clearwater.text: One more on this front: who actually owns the patient records — the clinic corporation, or do individual practitioners retain any ownership of charts for patients they treat?

The corporation owns all the patient records — that's explicit in our associate agreements and it's been that way since we incorporated. When a practitioner joins, they acknowledge that any clinical notes they create in ClinicNest belong to Clearwater Physiotherapy & Wellness Inc. We're the custodian under Alberta's HIA, and honestly it has to be that way for continuity of care and our direct-billing obligations. If someone leaves, they don't take charts with them, though we'll forward records to another clinic if a patient requests it in writing. Right now we've got about 3,900 active patient charts in the system.
Shifting to the team structure: of your 11 physiotherapists, how many are T4 employees versus independent contractors?

Sorry, I misspoke a second ago: it's about 4,300 active patient charts, not 3,900. On the PTs, honestly I think you already have that from the roster: three of us are on T4, me, Leah and Marcus, and the other eight are associates on contractor agreements.
And the six RMTs — are they all on signed contractor agreements, or are any on the older 2019 form like Hannah?

All six RMTs are on the same 2022 contractor agreement, all signed, none on the old form. And just so you understand why I want to drop to two days a week after the sale: my dad was diagnosed with Parkinson's last year and I'm helping my mom with his care, but keep that out of the book please.

That goes to your broker only, never the sale document.

Beyond Ethan Marsh leaving last October, have any other PTs or RMTs left in the past three years?
Just Ethan, really, plus one RMT who moved to Edmonton in 2023 for family reasons. Sorry, I have to run, I've got a patient in five minutes. Can we pick this up tomorrow?

Of course — we've covered a lot of ground. Before you go, the one thing I'd most like to confirm is whether both clinic premises are zoned for healthcare or therapy use. A quick yes now, or shall we start there next time?
Let's start there next time, I really have to go now.
Absolutely — we'll pick up with the zoning question next time. Everything's saved, and your broker will follow up with Dana on the insurer agreements and IPAC documentation. Talk soon.

Good to pick up where we left off — last time we got through the team's forward plans and some of the compliance history. One thing that came up in your broker notes: the call notes show a preference not to sell to Bowmont — can you tell me a bit more about what's behind that?

Yeah, honestly they're the one buyer I'd really rather avoid. They tried to poach Leah last fall — offered her more money and equity in a new clinic they were opening near Hillhurst — and the whole approach felt pretty aggressive. We matched the comp to keep her, but the bigger thing is Bowmont runs a volume model: fifteen-minute follow-ups, double-booking, treat-and-street. That's the opposite of what we've built here. If they bought us they'd gut the culture in six months, and I think we'd lose half the team. I'd much rather see this go to an independent buyer or a smaller group that actually values the forty-five-minute model and wants to keep the people who made this place work.

On Leah specifically — given the Bowmont situation last fall and her importance to the concussion program, is there any retention arrangement being discussed for her as part of the sale, or would that be left to the buyer to negotiate?

That's really up to the buyer, you know? I can't bind her to anything beyond what's already in her employment contract, and honestly I haven't told her about the sale yet. What I can do is introduce the new owner properly, explain the transition, and make it clear that keeping Leah is critical. She's got a two-year rolling non-compete in her contract — five kilometers, which covers most of the northwest — so she can't just walk across the street. But retention bonuses, equity, whatever the buyer wants to offer, that's their call. I'll stay involved long enough to help with that conversation if it helps.
Does Alberta require that a buyer of the clinic be a licensed physiotherapist, or can a non-PT — like a corporate consolidator or investor group — own the shares?

No, Alberta doesn't require the owner to be a PT. The College of Physiotherapists of Alberta regulates practitioners, not ownership. You just need a designated clinical director who is a licensed physio — right now that's me, but it could be Leah or Marcus or whoever the buyer brings in. So a corporate buyer or an investor group can absolutely own the shares, they just need someone with an Alberta PT license to be accountable for clinical standards and college compliance. That's actually part of why I think this is attractive to a range of buyers, not just other clinicians.
Are both clinic locations confirmed to be zoned for healthcare or therapy use, or is there any risk the zoning wouldn't transfer cleanly to a new owner?
